title: Sidelines and move-order tricks
intro:
Everything that is not 2.d4 d5 followed by one of the four main choices. None of it is dangerous, and all of it is worth ten minutes so that you are never surprised on move two.

## The Fantasy Variation, 3.f3

White props up e4 with a pawn and hopes for an open f-file later. The critical answer is 3...dxe4 4.fxe4 e5, hitting d4 at once, and it is sharp enough that both sides need to know it. This course plays the quiet 3...e6 instead: build the wall, pin the knight with ...Bb4, trade it off, and only then take on e4. With the f-pawn gone from f3, ...Qh4+ arrives with check and wins the pawn on e4 back at once, and White's king never castles.

## The Two Knights, 2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3

White develops both knights and delays d4. The answer is 3...Bg4, and the point is that the bishop gets out and then trades itself for the knight on f3. Black gives up the bishop pair and gets a completely solid position with no weaknesses, which is a fine bargain when White has no way to open the game.

## The King's Indian Attack, 2.d3

White is not fighting for the centre at all, so take it: 2...d5 3.Nd2 e5. Black has two pawns in the middle and free development, which is more than the Caro-Kann normally promises.

## Transpositions

Most sidelines turn into a main chapter after a move or two. 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4 is chapter 1. 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.d4 is chapter 2. 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.d4 is chapter 3. Recognising this is most of the work: play the move you would play there.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Taking on e4 too early against the Fantasy, before ...Bb4 has provoked a weakness. Answering 4.h3 in the Two Knights with ...Bh5, when 5.g4 costs Black the bishop's freedom for nothing. Treating 2.d3 as harmless and playing passively, instead of taking the centre with ...e5. And, generally, playing a sideline by feel rather than steering it into the chapter you already know.
